# Diagnosing A/C Compressor Load on a 1984 Toyota Carina

When an engine idles smoothly but revs up or stalls immediately upon engaging the air conditioning, the issue is almost always mechanical load rather than software. In your specific case with the 1984 Toyota Carina AA60, the symptoms point directly to a hydraulic or friction problem within the compressor assembly itself. The "click click" noise you hear when accelerating, combined with the feeling of high engine load during traffic, suggests the clutch is engaging, but the internal mechanism is fighting back against rotation.

The fact that the A/C belt tension and clutch operation appear normal rules out simple slippage or a failed magnetic switch. When you engage the A/C, the system demands significant torque to compress refrigerant gas. If the compressor oil is degraded, contaminated with moisture, or simply low on volume, the internal bearings seize momentarily under load. This creates a sudden spike in drag that the idle speed control cannot compensate for fast enough, resulting in the stalling behavior you described. The noise likely stems from the piston rings dragging against cylinder walls or a stuck valve train inside the compressor head as it tries to build pressure against an obstruction or insufficient lubrication.

You mentioned your friend suggesting an issue with the "gas" inside the compressor. While phrasing is imprecise, the underlying concept is correct: the state of the refrigerant charge matters, but more critically, the condition of the oil trapped within that charge matters. Over time, refrigerant can absorb moisture from the atmosphere if seals degrade. When this moist gas enters the compressor and undergoes compression, it can freeze inside the valve pockets or mix with the oil to create sludge. This sludge acts like a hydraulic lock, preventing the pistons from moving freely when the clutch engages.

Before tearing apart the compressor, inspect the accumulator or receiver-drier located on the low-pressure side of the system. On older Toyotas like your AA60, these units often become clogged with debris or their desiccant turns saturated, leading to liquid refrigerant returning to the compressor (slugging). If liquid hits the moving parts instead of gas, it creates a massive, immediate load spike that mimics a seized engine. Check for ice buildup on the lines; while this can indicate low charge, it is also a common symptom of restricted airflow or a failing expansion valve.

If the refrigerant level looks correct but the noise persists, the internal components of the compressor are likely worn. The "click click" sound you hear during acceleration might be the clutch pulley slipping slightly due to excessive heat generated by the friction inside the compressor, or it could be the alternator belt jumping if the engine is struggling so hard it dips in RPM. However, given that the load feels heavy specifically when the A/C is on, the culprit is almost certainly the compressor internals.

Replacing the unit with a remanufactured assembly from a reputable supplier is often the most cost-effective route for an 1984 model, as finding new OEM parts is difficult. Ensure you replace the O-rings and seals during installation. If you choose to rebuild it yourself, verify that the new oil mix contains the correct amount of viscosity modifiers for your specific climate; using too little oil will lead to premature bearing failure under high load conditions.

Finally, consider monitoring your engine's idle speed control valve (ISC). As the ECU attempts to raise RPMs to compensate for the A/C load, if the ISC is clogged with carbon depositsâa common issue on older carbureted or early fuel-injected Toyotasâthe engine may not reach the target idle speed before the compressor demand exceeds the available torque. Cleaning the ISC and its solenoid port can sometimes resolve the stalling without needing to replace the compressor entirely.
